claims.text: HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 786 MPa yield strength.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 1314 MPa compressive strength.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 13.5% terminal strain.
Adding approximately 1–2 wt% oxygen during synthesis will promote in situ oxide formation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The oxygen addition will produce uniformly distributed nanometric oxide precipitates at grain boundaries.
The oxide particles will stabilize grain boundaries.
The oxide particles will delay crack initiation during tensile deformation.
The oxide particles will impede rapid crack propagation during tensile deformation.
The grain-boundary oxide particles will not interfere with lattice strengthening.
Grain-boundary stabilization and impeded cracking will permit more uniform plastic tensile strain and improve ductility.
Oxygen modification will increase uniform tensile elongation by approximately 20–30%, to about 16–17%.
The modified alloy's yield strength will remain within approximately 10% of 786 MPa.
The modified alloy's compressive strength will remain within approximately 10% of 1314 MPa.
Oxygen modification will preserve impact-triggered energy release.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has previously demonstrated high energy release upon impact.
The predicted tensile benefit applies at room temperature under quasi-static loading below 10^-3 s^-1.
Excessive or poorly controlled oxygen may cause embrittlement rather than a beneficial oxide dispersion.

contradictions.description: The reported 13.5% terminal strain is associated with the compression-focused baseline, but the prediction treats it as the baseline for uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and tensile uniform elongation are different quantities and cannot be directly equated without tensile baseline data.

The baseline attributes demonstrated impact-triggered high-energy release to HfZrTiTa0.53, although no cited record is supplied for that alloy's impact-energy behavior; the stated prior energetic result in the task concerns WFeNiMo fragments rather than this alloy.
